catalog_quote: Accent is phonemic. Accent usually occurs on the final syllable of a word, though there are many exceptions to this trend, especially in words that have been borrowed from Tagalog, Spanish and English*. An accented syllable always has the peak of the intonation contour. A final accented syllable is usually stressed (loudest) and the syllable before it is shortened. An accented penult is always lengthened. In this section, non-final accented syllables are marked by the symbol (') preceding that syllable. Except for a small number of words with accent on the antepenult, the vast majority of words have accent either on the ultima or the penult. There are quite a number of pairs of words which differ only by accent. [p. 5:] anak child / 'anak children ... sulat lime container / 'sulat letter ... salinan ko I will pass by. / sa'linan ko I will change it. ... It is noteworthy that all of the instances of word pairs differing by accent have only a single consonant between the ultima and penult. Words which have a consonant cluster between the ultima and penult do not seem to show a contrast in the placement of accent. Words of the pattern CVCCV (with final glottal stop) invariably have accent on the penult. Words of the pattern CVCCVC are pronounced in everyday speech sometimes with an accented ultima and sometimes with an accented penult, and both of these by the same person.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is contrastive (lexical) within a final two-syllable window: the default and statistically dominant position is the final syllable, but many words (native and especially loans) have penultimate accent, realized as vowel length on the penult, and a handful have antepenultimate accent; minimal pairs such as anak 'child' vs 'anak 'children', sulat 'lime container' vs 'sulat 'letter' exist. The dictionary marks only non-final accent, treating final accent as the unmarked default.
new_statements.exceptions: All accent minimal pairs have a single intervocalic consonant; words with a medial consonant cluster show no accent contrast: CVCCV (with final glottal stop) words invariably have penult accent, and CVCCVC words vary freely between ultima and penult accent even within one speaker (dictionary records the more common variant). Loans from Tagalog, Spanish and English are frequent exceptions to the final-accent trend. A small number of words have antepenultimate accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word (citation forms and dictionary headwords); accent described phonetically as intonation peak plus loudness (final) or length (penult); phrase-level examples (salinan ko / sa'linan ko; megtabasek / meg'tabasek) show the contrast persists in affixed forms and short sentences.
new_statements.identity_note: Headland & Healey (1974) and Headland & Headland (1974) describe 'Casiguran Dumagat', the speech of the Agta Negritos of the San Ildefonso Peninsula / Casiguran, Aurora (Quezon) -- the Casiguran Agta half of Glottolog's Casiguran-Nagtipunan Agta (casi1235, ISO dgc); Nagtipunan Agta (the western variety reported by Robinson & Lobel) is not covered. The authors note mutually intelligible Palanan Agta and Paranan dialects to the north (separate Glottolog languoids). Rosetta Project's 'rosettaproject_dgc_book-1' (Healey 1960, An Agta Grammar) is misfiled under dgc: it describes Central Cagayan Agta, not Casiguran.

Tagalog/Spanish/English loans); accented syllable carries intonation peak; final accented syllable is loudest, accented penult is lengthened; a few antepenult-accented words; minimal pairs anak/'anak etc; CVCCV(+glottal) words always penult-accented; CVCCVC words vary freely between ultima and penult accent.
